gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the MacBook Neo, the likely student Mac, sends video from only one of its two USB-C ports (the USB 3 port; the USB 2 port has no DisplayPort), or that macOS only mirrors screens split off one cable by MST. On a Neo or a base M1/M2 Air, a dual extender that needs no driver can extend to one added screen at most.
standout_why: I compared against three cited pages. Macworld's 'Best Portable Monitors for Mac' (cited) says base M1 and M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo drive only one monitor, and that the Trio 3 Pro needs 'free software (rather like DisplayLink)' on them. It says nothing about which Neo port carries video and nothing about MST or mirroring. iTechGuides' '15 Best Laptop Screen Extenders for 2026' (cited) says the USB-C port must support DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt or USB4. It also says a triple kit 'may show one working display, duplicate screens'. It gives no per-Mac display counts and never mentions MST. TechRepublic (cited) returned HTTP 403, so I could not compare it. The one-display limit is partly covered already. The Neo port detail and the MST mirroring rule are new.
decides: For a student on a MacBook Neo or a base M1/M2 MacBook Air, the pick is one added screen on a single USB-C cable plugged into the port that carries video (on the Neo, the USB 3 port). A two-screen extender gives only one extended screen without a display driver, and macOS will not split one cable into two extended screens over MST. On an M4 or M5 MacBook Air (Apple: up to two external displays), a two-screen extender can run natively from two Thunderbolt ports. So the page should send the screen-count choice through the shopper's laptop model first, as ChatGPT's own follow-up question hinted.

findings.label: MacBook Neo external displays
findings.value: 1 external display, up to 4K at 60 Hz, with the built-in display at full native resolution
findings.note: Apple's US spec page: 'Supports one external display with up to a native resolution of 4K at 60Hz'. Chip listed as Apple A18 Pro.

findings.label: MacBook Neo: which port carries video
findings.value: Only the USB 3 (USB-C) port supports DisplayPort (native DisplayPort 1.4, up to HBR3); the second port, USB 2 (USB-C), handles charging and USB 2 data but no DisplayPort
findings.note: From the Ports section of Apple's US spec page. A native (Alt Mode) screen plugged into the USB 2 port gets no picture, which I infer from Apple's port list.

findings.label: MacBook Air (M5) external displays
findings.value: Up to 2 external displays (two at up to 6K 60 Hz or 4K 144 Hz), including two over a single Thunderbolt port, with the built-in display at full native resolution
findings.source_title: MacBook Air 13- and 15-inch (M5) - Technical Specifications - Apple
findings.note: Apple's spec page does not say lid open or closed. Macworld (below) says base M4 and M5 Airs drive two with the lid open.

findings.label: External display limit by MacBook Air chip
findings.value: M1 and M2: 1; M3: 2 only with the lid closed; M4 and M5: 2 with the lid open; MacBook Neo: 1
findings.source_title: Get around Apple's annoying M1/M2/M3/M4/M5/Neo Mac external display limitations via software and adapters (Macworld, updated Nov 19, 2026)
findings.note: Macworld: M3 'Maximum two external displays if MacBook lid is closed'; base M4 and M5 Air 'do natively support two displays with the lid open'; DisplayLink 'requires a third-party driver to be installed on the Mac'. This Macworld article was not among ChatGPT's results; the cited Macworld page covers only the M1/M2/Neo one-monitor limit.

findings.label: M1/M2 native external display path (Plugable)
findings.value: Base M1/M2: 1 external display via Thunderbolt up to 6K 60 Hz; base M4 and M5: 2 via Thunderbolt
findings.source_title: Understanding External Display Support on Apple M1, M2, M3, M4 and M5 Chips (Plugable, Aug 28, 2026)
findings.note: Plugable names USB DisplayLink docks and adapters as the way past the native limit.

findings.label: macOS and MST (one cable split to several screens)
findings.value: macOS mirrors at best: an MST hub runs only in 'Mirrored' mode, and daisy-chained or hub displays show as clones, not extended screens
findings.source_title: Can TS3 and TS3 Plus support DisplayPort Multi-Stream Transport (MST) feature? - CalDigit Support Center
findings.note: CalDigit: 'MacOS does not currently support MST, and will be able to mirror monitors at best.' Tiled MST (one monitor) is the only MST macOS fully supports. So on a Mac, a dual extender run from one cable without a driver cannot extend to two different screens.

findings.label: Video path on base M1/M2/Neo Macs
findings.value: Needs Mobile Pixels' software installed on those Macs
findings.note: Macworld: 'To work with the Trio 3 Pro users of those Macs will need to download and install free software (rather like DisplayLink).' Rival page already states this.

findings.label: Mac driver install rule
findings.value: Mac driver for Trio Series 2nd and 3rd Gen; install it before plugging the screen into the Mac
findings.source_title: Download Drivers - Mobile Pixels (macOS installation guide for Trio Series 2nd Gen & 3rd Gen)
findings.note: Page warning: 'DO NOT plug the Mobile Pixels Inc Device into your mac before executing the driver installation.' Separate downloads for macOS 14 and later, 13-11, 10.15 and 10.14-10.9. The page does not say what the driver enables.
